course: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional (AIP-C01)
part_title: Lab 02 — Diagnose Bedrock Converse API Schema and Response Errors
review_basis: Six original Module 19 WebP images slides 06–11 directly reviewed; full 74-slide local image audit successful and simulator guidance consulted.

scenes.title: Scenario and request path
scenes.narration: The failure starts at the application, not at the model playground. Trace the user to the boto3 client, Bedrock Runtime Converse API and selected foundation model. The example has two symptoms: an HTTP 400 ValidationException, or a 200 response that the application fails to parse. First record the model identifier, AWS Region, request ID and actual exception in the application's CloudWatch logs. The illustrated failing request reports that messages zero content must be an array of content blocks. That gives us an initial request-schema hypothesis, not an IAM finding. Check the complete request before granting permissions. The request should include a supported model or inference profile, a messages list, and within each user message a content array of typed entries such as text. The Bedrock console model selector helps confirm availability, but a successful playground response is not proof that the application sends the same structured body. Compare the application's actual request and the response content path. Our goal is to distinguish malformed input, a parser regression, access denial, model-region mismatch and throttling, and repair only the failing layer.

scenes.title: Classify error codes before changing permissions
scenes.narration: Look at the four error panels and treat them as a diagnostic decision tree, not four interchangeable failures. A 400 ValidationException such as invalid content shape means inspect the Converse input contract first. A 403 AccessDeniedException means examine the execution role, model access and scoped authorization. A 404 ResourceNotFoundException may indicate an invalid model identifier or model availability in the chosen Region. A 429 ThrottlingException points toward request pressure, quotas and bounded retry behavior. Open the application log and record the full exception message and request ID. The screenshot of the Bedrock model access screen is supporting evidence for the access branch only; it is not a universal fix for every error. For 400, compare JSON with the API schema. For 403, check the actual principal and permissions. For 404, cross-check the selected Region and model or inference profile. For 429, investigate admission rate and safe jitter backoff. Do not use wildcard policies, blind retries or model changes to conceal an invalid request.

scenes.title: Inspect and repair request contract
scenes.narration: The left code illustration passes a bare string as a user message's content value. The resulting 400 is expected because Converse requires an array of content blocks. The corrected middle example wraps the string in a list containing an object with a text property. Open the simulated application's request settings and change only that malformed body structure. Now inspect the right response example: on HTTP 200, the returned assistant text sits inside output, message, and a content array. The stopReason reports end_turn in this illustrative successful response. The application must parse the new structured output instead of expecting an old completion string. Use the Bedrock playground sample as a comparison, but validate the same SDK call in the application. Confirm the status and returned JSON after the repair. If you still see 400, inspect the exact serialized message again; if it changes to 403 or 404, follow that separate evidence branch. The lowest table reminds you that each status requires a distinct remedy.

scenes.title: Parse response content blocks safely
scenes.narration: This slide demonstrates a complete boto3 Converse request and text extraction procedure. Build a bedrock-runtime client for the chosen Region, call converse with the supported model ID and a typed messages array, then inspect response dot output dot message dot content. It is a list of blocks, not a single completion string. Iterate over those blocks, extract text only when the block has a text field, and handle other supported block types such as tool use explicitly. The lower sample shows the assistant content array and the parsed text, Hello, how can I help you today. This is what a successful application parser should display. If the service returns HTTP 200 but the app shows nothing, compare the actual response structure to the parser's access path. The model catalog image helps verify the selected model and Region, but does not repair client-side parsing. Add a regression fixture with multiple content blocks and another without a text block. Success means the application safely handles each permitted response shape without incorrectly treating non-text content as an answer.

scenes.title: Check model region and scoped permissions separately
scenes.narration: Start on the left by confirming model or inference profile availability in the actual region used by the SDK, illustrated as us-east-1. Next inspect the real execution identity in IAM Roles, rather than a developer's interactive console identity. The sample role policy shows a scoped Bedrock invocation permission on a model resource. Confirm that the allowed action, resource ARN, model or inference-profile usage and policy conditions match the application's request. Do not copy the illustrative ARN literally, and do not broaden access for schema or throttling errors. Finally run a minimal known-good Converse request using the same region and model identifier. The right-hand example returns HTTP 200 and typed text content. If a 403 persists, collect permission evidence from the exact principal and request. If a 404 persists, recheck model identifier and Region. If a 400 persists, return to the messages content shape. The error examples at the bottom make those branches explicit. Each test should change just one cause, preserving security and keeping the result reproducible.

scenes.title: Verify positive and malformed-request tests
scenes.narration: The final slide is a two-sided regression test. In the positive case, construct a valid user message with a list of typed text content blocks, send it through boto3 Converse and verify HTTP 200. The output must contain an assistant message with a content array that the application successfully parses; an API success without parsed output is incomplete recovery. Next deliberately submit a malformed message whose content is an object rather than an array. The expected outcome is a clear ValidationException, HTTP 400, with an appropriate request identifier, rather than a retry or misleading AccessDenied. Keep separate negative fixtures for an unauthorized model invocation, an unavailable model-region combination and throttling under controlled conditions; the response classes should remain distinguishable. Add client-side request validation and parser regression tests to the release gate. In the test log record model, Region, request shape, status code and parsed output. Remove temporary policy changes after testing. The lab is complete only when both valid and intentionally invalid requests behave predictably.
